Learning the seams

Plasma simulations are stitched together from models that each stop somewhere. Whatever crosses the seam is set by a rule of thumb. The plan: learn what crosses it from the expensive model, use it inside the cheap one, and know when not to trust it. Mostly pictures.

The plan · RISE in one picture

Two seams, one recipe, three aims

Aim 1 · kinetic → fluid. Learn the ion pressure anisotropy from Sironi's kinetic dynamo runs, and make it work inside a running MHD code.

Aim 2 · core ↔ edge. Use the TCV edge foundation model as the edge of the TORAX core code.

Aim 3 · knowing when it is wrong. A calibrated trust score decides when to call the expensive model (chapter 10).

Aim 1 · Chapter 1 · The physics

Squeeze a flux tube and the plasma stops being a fluid

In a hot, nearly collisionless plasma each ion spirals around the magnetic field. When the field strengthens, the spiral tightens and the ion's motion across the field gets hotter (T⊥ grows with B). Motion along the field cools at the same time. Ideal MHD keeps one temperature, so it never sees this. The plasma does, and once the imbalance gets large enough, tiny instabilities (mirror and firehose) switch on and push it back. Drag the field strength and watch.

The flux tube

Field lines bunch together where B is strong. The circle is one ion's orbit across the field; its size tracks the perpendicular speed over B.

The ions' velocity spread

A fluid assumes a round spread (dashed). Width = spread along the field, height = spread across it.

Where this puts the plasma

Grey cloud: where the real kinetic simulation (unseen 125 di box) actually sits. Red and blue lines: mirror and firehose limits. The dot is your tube; the faint path is every B you could pick.

What the fluid code should feel

A bent field line pulls itself straight (magnetic tension). Extra parallel pressure weakens that pull; at the firehose limit it vanishes and the line goes floppy. MHD always uses factor 1.

Why this matters. The imbalance acts like a viscosity: it resists stretching the field. It also changes how bent the field lines get, which controls how cosmic rays scatter. A fluid code needs a rule for it, a closure. The classic rules are "zero" (MHD), "pinned at the stability limits", or a Braginskii-type formula. Our question is whether a model trained on kinetic simulations does better, and how far it can be trusted.

ρ dU/dt = −∇(p⊥ + B²/8π) + ∇·[ (B²/4π + p⊥ − p∥) b̂b̂ ] ← the learned closure supplies p⊥ − p∥
Aim 1 · Chapter 2 · New · the data

The kinetic boxes are dynamos

Seven of Sironi's driven runs (mass ratio 16–256, boxes 31–125 di). (a) The field grows by about 10³ in energy and is still growing in the test window (+37% from snapshot 180 to 200 at mi/me = 64). (c) The temperature stays roughly flat because the code caps particle momenta. Grey: training snapshots; blue: test.

So the fair test of a fluid model is whether it keeps this dynamo going, not whether it matches one frame (chapter 7).

The imbalance in a kinetic simulation, and what each closure guesses

A 2D slice through a 64³ crop of Lorenzo's TRISTAN-MP dynamo runs, smoothed to one ion skin depth. Red: hotter across the field (mirror side). Blue: hotter along it (firehose side). Each panel is a closure's guess using only density, flow and B. The number is the error as a % of the natural variation: 0% is perfect, about 100% is no better than guessing the average.

Aim 1 · Chapter 4 · Where the plasma lives

Every cell of the box on one map

Each cell of the box is placed by its β∥ (pressure over magnetic pressure) and its temperature ratio. The kinetic plasma fills a wedge bounded by the instability lines, and some of it leaks past them. A good closure should fill the same wedge, including the edges.

Kinetic simulation

Closure

x: log10 β∥ from −0.5 to 2.7. y: log10(T⊥/T∥) from −0.8 to 0.8. Darker = more cells. Red curve: mirror limit 1+1/β∥. Blue curve: firehose limit 1−2/β∥.

Share of the box past each limit

Every closure misses part of the firehose tail. Note how much of the smoothed simulation sits past the mirror line: a closure that hard-pins the plasma at the limit is wrong by construction.

Aim 1 · Chapter 5 · Does it transfer

Trust falls with distance from the training data, unless the model keeps rebuilding everything

Three kinds of distance. Mass ratio: real protons are 1836× heavier than electrons, and our training runs stop at 115. Shot: a different TCV discharge. Blur: how coarse the fluid grid is compared with the ion skin depth.

Mass ratio · astro

Closure skill (1 = exact, 0 = flat guess) on runs never seen in training, box fixed at 23.3 di. Models that also rebuild every other field hold at the real proton mass; models fitted only to the closure fall to a flat guess.

New discharge · fusion

TCV edge, pretrained on shot 85604, adapted to 85606. Error in integrated particle transport (reconstructing held-out frames) against the share of the new shot's frames used. Spacing is categorical; 100% = 432 frames.

Blur · astro

Closure error against the coarse-graining scale (lower is better). Our per-scale networks degrade as the blur grows, while the Braginskii-type rule stays flat. For the real-mass run the crop is only about 9 di, so 4 and 8 di are not shown.

Aim 1 · Chapter 6 · Does it push the plasma right

A fluid code feels the imbalance only as a force

A pretty map is not enough. The fluid code needs the divergence of the anisotropic pressure, the extra push in the equation from chapter 1. These tests turn each closure's prediction into that push and compare it with the push from the simulation's own pressures. Then one test drops the trained networks into a small MHD solver and lets it run.

Error in the push

Mean-squared error of the anisotropic force, relative to leaving it out (MHD = 100%). Six snapshots per run, 48³ region. The training-regime run (mime64, 62.5 di) and an unseen bigger box (mime16, 125 di). The pinned-at-limits rule makes the push worse than leaving it out.

Inside a running fluid code

25 steps of a small isothermal MHD solver with the networks recomputed every step (no true fields supplied). It stays stable: density stays positive and mass is conserved to 10⁻⁷. The run covers only 0.7 di/c, so this shows the plumbing works, not that the trajectory is more accurate.

Aim 1 · Chapter 7 · New · the real test

Running the closure inside a stirred MHD copy of the kinetic box

Same box, same stirring as the kinetic run, started from a stirred kinetic snapshot. The closure is recomputed from the evolving MHD state, and nothing from the kinetic run is fed in after the start.

The kinetic run survives its strong stirring only because its thermostat caps particle momenta. MHD has no such cap, so its flows pass c within two snapshots (red). The stirring strength is tuned once on plain MHD to the kinetic energy, then frozen for every closure.

First look, one snapshot, before tuning. Inside MHD, the learned closure keeps the kinetic spread of anisotropy (c); the pinned rule collapses onto two lines (b). The sharp lower edge in (c) is a firehose clip that keeps the equations well posed.

Already visible: plain MHD loses about half its magnetic energy over the stretch where the kinetic dynamo holds its field. That's the gap the closure must close. Full runs (3 closures × 3 stirring histories) are on the cluster. running

Aim 1 · Chapter 8 · New · exploratory

The electric field MHD is missing

At the ion scale MHD also misses part of the electric field (b). The Hall term, free in any fluid code, explains about 90% of it (c). But all of the field-energy loss sits in the remainder (d, e). It's not a resistivity: one coefficient matches the mean but not where it happens (g, r = 0.41), and about a third of the volume gives energy back (h). Whether a second closure can learn this from these runs is an open test.

Aim 2 · Chapter 9 · New · the core–edge seam

Our TCV edge emulator as the edge of the TORAX core code

TORAX's edge slot hands over the power leaving the core and the separatrix density, and takes back the separatrix temperature. Today it holds a formula (Lengyel); the emulator goes in its place. The emulator's own separatrix is radial cell 16, so Te,sep is read straight off its prediction.

Input. The core's state enters as the observed strip at the emulator's inner boundary, the same masked reconstruction it was pretrained on. Losses stay general and pixel-based; the separatrix temperature is only a readout.

Data. The emulator has seen one core condition. To make it respond to the core: a JAX-Hermes3 scan of core power and fueling, roughly 130–150 A100-hours once the 85604 setup is ported. The second discharge, 85606, stays held out for the final test.

Aim 3 · Chapter 10 · The routing dream

Use the cheapest model that is good enough, and know when it isn't

The long-term machine has three rungs. A learned emulator jumps ahead fast. A fluid solver with a learned closure handles most of the volume. Kinetic patches supply truth where the closure is unsure. A router reads a trust signal and decides, region by region, which rung to pay for. Everything we have done so far is a piece of this.

exists and testedfirst test onlynot built yet

The first routing test: send the most doubtful regions to the expensive physics

The 48³ test region cut into 216 cubes (6 slices of 6×6). Shade = how wrong the learned push is there (average over six snapshots). Outlined cubes are the ones a perfect router would send to the kinetic code at this budget.

Remaining force error against the volume sent to the kinetic code. Picking regions where two of our models disagree beats picking at random by 15–17% at 20%. The "perfect router" line knows the true error and sets the ceiling. This is an offline test: no speed-up or live coupling is measured.

Chapter 11 · What the literature already did

The pieces exist separately; the combination is the open part

A rough map, placed by hand. Left to right: is the correction fitted to snapshots, or trained inside the running solver? Bottom to top: is there one fixed model, or does the method decide where to spend expensive physics? Click a dot.

The defensible gap. Kinetic-informed closures exist (resistivity, viscosity, heat flux). Closures trained inside differentiable solvers exist. Routing between fidelities exists for near-equilibrium plasmas and tokamak surrogates. The test nobody has run is whether a broadly pretrained representation makes turbulent-plasma corrections transfer better once they are trained inside the solver, and whether its own uncertainty can route between rungs, in two very different plasmas.
